body:
Tested locally on Windows with Python 3.14.8, it works as expected.

Binary size comparison for Windows x86_64 optimized editor (MSVC 2022):

- `master`: 169,884,672 bytes
- This PR: 152,225,792 bytes

Zipped size for each:

- `master`: 82,223,821 bytes
- This PR: 64,588,993 bytes

According to https://godot-size-history.github.io/, this change alone should bring the editor Windows ZIP size below the one of Godot 4.4's.
We also use the same zlib compression for the certificates and some other data, difference is much smaller, but changing all to zstd can save additional 500KB.
How slower is "much slower"? How often are the translations changed/built anew?

> How slower is "much slower"?

Translation headers generation takes 36 seconds in total on M4 Pro Mac. I have not measured time before the change.

> How often are the translations changed/built anew?

Should only happen when translation files or related scripts change.

Tested on Linux using the latest version of the [official SDK](https://github.com/godotengine/buildroot/releases/tag/godot-2026.05.x-1) (which uses Python 3.14.6).

Build command: `PATH=/path/to/x86_64-godot-linux-gnu_sdk-buildroot/bin:$PATH scons -j8 target=editor production=yes`

- `master`: 145,062,104 bytes
- PR: 126,859,480 bytes

Using maximum ZIP compression:

- `master`: 75,933,579 bytes
- PR: 59,215,000 bytes

Did not measure time to build translations.
Changed it to use level 20 compression only if `production=yes` is set to speed up debug builds (uses default compression level == 3).

Overall I think this is a great change. I'll do some tests for the actual impact on compilation time.
One small concern is making `zstandard` a new hard dependency, which may cause some minor friction. We could consider falling back to Deflate if we want to make it smoother (that would imply also encoding which format to use to decompress).

So I've done some fine-tuning of the compression to find good tradeoffs on compilation speed vs size reduction. I also tried enabling long-distance matching (LDM) which yields significant gains.

| Dataset (raw) | before (deflate-9) | PR non-prod (zstd-3) | PR prod (zstd-20) | tuning non-prod (zstd-7+LDM) | tuning prod (zstd-18+LDM) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| editor translations (18.1 MB) | 0.56s → 4.57 MB | 0.06s → 3.68 MB | 7.80s → 2.41 MB | 0.27s → 3.04 MB | 6.17s → 2.44 MB |
| doc translations (96.1 MB) | 2.38s → 20.63 MB | 0.32s → 20.27 MB | 47.32s → 8.55 MB | 1.08s → 11.69 MB | 35.23s → 8.66 MB |
| doc/classes (8.4 MB) | 0.13s → 1.40 MB | 0.02s → 1.34 MB | 3.24s → 0.93 MB | 0.08s → 1.13 MB | 2.11s → 0.946 MB |
| property translations (5.3 MB) | 0.17s → 1.31 MB | 0.02s → 1.10 MB | 1.64s → 0.80 MB | 0.06s → 0.96 MB | 1.49s → 0.80 MB |
| extractable translations (151 KB) | 0.002s → 29.3 KB | 0.000s → 32.0 KB | 0.06s → 26.6 KB | 0.001s → 29.5 KB | 0.039s → 26.6 KB |
| certs / ca-bundle.crt (186 KB) | 0.003s → 108.9 KB | 0.001s → 105.3 KB | 0.03s → 103.0 KB | 0.002s → 103.6 KB | 0.024s → 102.9 KB |
| gdextension interface dump (328 KB) | 0.002s → 20.9 KB | 0.000s → 24.7 KB | 0.08s → 17.6 KB | 0.002s → 21.1 KB | 0.032s → 18.3 KB |
| **Total** | **3.25s → 28.07 MB** | **0.42s → 26.55 MB (−5.4%)** | **60.17s → 12.84 MB (−54.3%)** | **1.50s → 16.97 MB (−39.5%)** | **45.13s → 12.99 MB (−53.7%)** |

So basically my changes would do:
- Non-production goes from 5.4% size cut in this PR to 39.5% with level 7 and LDM, for an extra second of build time (only on translation changes, which is very rare). LDM allows us to get much better gains while increasing the compression level a bit.
- Production size gains are consistent but 25% faster (15s saved) which may add up for full official production builds. LDM allows us to get basically the same gains with a lower compression level.

```diff
commit 019307aaf69fef9445c9e42c3746683d5650d2f0
Author: Rémi Verschelde <rverschelde@gmail.com>
Date:   Tue Oct 13 18:26:43 2026 +0200

    SCons: Fine-tune zstd compression for good size/speed tradeoffs
    
    - Production: Use level 18 with long-distance matching, cuts compression
      time in half for a similar size gain.
    - Non-production: Use level 7 with long-distance-matching, increases
      compression time by less than a second for a very significant size gain.

diff --git a/methods.py b/methods.py
index 1105097656..0e1e66b459 100644
--- a/methods.py
+++ b/methods.py
@@ -1582,18 +1582,24 @@ def get_buffer(path: str) -> bytes:
 
 
 def compress_buffer_zstd(buffer: bytes, env):
-    level = 20 if env["production"] else 3
+    # Levels selected for a good tradeoff between compression speed and size reduction,
+    # being more aggressive on production builds.
+    # Long-distance matching helps a lot with the editor translations.
+    level = 18 if env["production"] else 7
     if sys.version_info >= (3, 14):
         import compression.zstd
 
-        return compression.zstd.compress(buffer, level)
+        CP = compression.zstd.CompressionParameter
+        options = {CP.compression_level: level, CP.enable_long_distance_matching: 1}
+        return compression.zstd.compress(buffer, options=options)
     else:
         try:
             import zstandard
         except ImportError:
             print_error("Python versions earlier than 3.14 require the `zstandard` module")
             sys.exit(255)
-        return zstandard.compress(buffer, level)
+        params = zstandard.ZstdCompressionParameters.from_level(level, enable_ldm=True)
+        return zstandard.ZstdCompressor(compression_params=params).compress(buffer)
 
 
 def compress_buffer(buffer: bytes) -> bytes:
```

I also looked into enabling some multi-threading but the gains weren't as clear.

To be comprehensive, here are the compression times and size gains for all zstd levels on my machine, for the two biggest datasets:

level | editor translations (18.1 MB) | doc translations (96.1 MB) | Total time / size | % size reduction vs. level 1
-- | -- | -- | -- | --
1 | 0.06s → 4.55 MB | 0.31s → 15.72 MB | 0.37s → 20.27 MB | —
2 | 0.08s → 3.98 MB | 0.38s → 15.24 MB | 0.46s → 19.22 MB | 5.2%
3 | 0.12s → 3.53 MB | 0.59s → 13.91 MB | 0.71s → 17.44 MB | 13.9%
4 | 0.15s → 3.44 MB | 0.65s → 13.52 MB | 0.80s → 16.96 MB | 16.3%
5 | 0.21s → 3.34 MB | 0.82s → 12.78 MB | 1.03s → 16.12 MB | 20.5%
6 | 0.23s → 3.16 MB | 0.96s → 12.26 MB | 1.19s → 15.42 MB | 23.9%
7 | 0.25s → 3.04 MB | 1.04s → 11.69 MB | 1.29s → 14.73 MB | 27.3%
8 | 0.27s → 2.97 MB | 1.19s → 11.41 MB | 1.46s → 14.38 MB | 29.0%
9 | 0.30s → 2.95 MB | 1.21s → 11.18 MB | 1.51s → 14.13 MB | 30.3%
10 | 0.37s → 2.88 MB | 1.54s → 10.77 MB | 1.91s → 13.65 MB | 32.7%
11 | 0.54s → 2.84 MB | 2.28s → 10.55 MB | 2.82s → 13.39 MB | 33.9%
12 | 0.65s → 2.83 MB | 2.5s → 10.47 MB | 3.15s → 13.30 MB | 34.4%
13 | 1.50s → 2.78 MB | 6.07s → 10.29 MB | 7.57s → 13.07 MB | 35.5%
14 | 1.72s → 2.74 MB | 8.57s → 10.12 MB | 10.29s → 12.86 MB | 36.6%
15 | 2.25s → 2.70 MB | 13.08s → 9.92 MB | 15.33s → 12.62 MB | 37.7%
16 | 4.0s → 2.50 MB | 21.5s → 9.12 MB | 25.5s → 11.62 MB | 42.7%
17 | 4.8s → 2.47 MB | 28.1s → 8.91 MB | 32.9s → 11.38 MB | 43.9%
18 | 5.8s → 2.44 MB | 31.8s → 8.66 MB | 37.6s → 11.10 MB | 45.2%
19 | 8.13s → 2.41 MB | 47.11s → 8.44 MB | 55.24s → 10.85 MB | 46.4%
20 | 8.26s → 2.41 MB | 50.30s → 8.40 MB | 58.56s → 10.81 MB | 46.7%
21 | 8.72s → 2.41 MB | 61.20s → 8.38 MB | 69.92s → 10.79 MB | 46.8%
22 | 9.02s → 2.41 MB | 73.89s → 8.35 MB | 82.91s → 10.76 MB | 46.9%

Since translations change very rarely (once a month or so), incremental rebuilds would smooth over this extra cost, so we could envision finding a single level that's good enough for both production and non-production.

Level 12 would bring us back to the same time as the previous Deflate compression, with a reduction from 20.27 MB to 13.30 MB. Then the gains aren't as good on level 13-15, would need to go to level 16 with 25.5s for 11.62 MB (so another 1.68 MB saved). As a reminder we're only talking editor binaries there, not templates, where saving a couple extra MB would be really worth any build time tradeoff. But again for production builds the extra time isn't that bad so level 18 is probably good.

Overall I'd say we could consider level 12 for non-production build, so people doing optimized but no-LTO builds with just `scons p=windows` would still have a good gains if they want to ship that build to users.

---

To clarify, all the measurements above were done with Python on the data we're compressing, but standalone, not as part of our SCons / editor build.

I should probably do a couple tests with a full editor build to confirm that the results are consistent.

Did some real build tests on our build servers.

The "incremental rebuild" times are measured after making a single line change to `doc/translations/fr.po` to force recompressing the doc translations, which is the biggest dataset. The time isn't representative of the compression time as it includes the usual SCons overhead + all the linking time, so what's relevant is the diff between tests.
But as mentioned in the footnote, I realized mid-way through that my methodology was flawed so those numbers aren't really useful.

## Non-production, optimized (`scons p=linux`)

| Branch | Full build | Incremental rebuild | Size |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Master | 3m01.0s | 22.6s | 152.30 MiB |
| PR (f9add79) | 3m02.2 s | 27.6s (+5.0s) | 148.07 MiB (-4.32 MiB) |
| Fine-tuning (level 7 + LDM) | 3m00.5s | 25.1s (+2.5s) | 138.90 (-13.40 MiB) |

## Non-production, dev build (`scons p=linux dev_build=yes fast_unsafe=yes`)

| Branch | Full build | Incremental rebuild | Size |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Master | 2m21.3s | 18.2s / 36.7s?[^1] | 1035.22 MiB |
| PR (f9add79) | 2m22.5s | 49.5s (+12.8s)[^1] | 1030.97 MiB (-4.25 MiB) |
| Fine-tuning (level 7 + LDM) | 2m20.4s | 46.7s (+10.0s)[^1] | 1021.81 MiB (-13.41 MiB) |

## Production build (`scons p=linux production=yes`)

| Branch | Full build | Incremental rebuild | Size |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Master | 4m03.6s | 20.1s? / 2m53.9s[^2] | 145.85 MiB |
| PR (f9add79) | 4m11.1s | - | 128.47 MiB (-17.38 MiB) |
| Fine-tuning (level 18 + LDM) | 4m03.5s | - | 128.62 MiB (-17.23 MiB) |

[^1]: I can't explain this, my first build tests linked fast, but then at some point it became slower. I don't see what changed on the build server to explain it. I tried incremental rebuilds with a change to `main.cpp` (leaving out compression related stuff) and it's also taking 37s, so it's not caused by the compression changes.
[^2]: That 20.1s result with LTO was surprising. I did see it regenerate `editor/translations/doc_translations.gen.h` but it didn't recompile `editor/translations/editor_translation.cpp` and thus didn't relink. That's when I realized that my incremental rebuild test wasn't very conclusive as I was just adding an empty line to `doc/translations/fr.po`, which isn't part of a `msgstr` and thus doesn't impact the compressed output... So all these numbers are worthless and I'm stopping this part of the comparison. The 2m53.9s one is after deleting the `.o` file for `editor_translation.cpp` to force a recompile and relink.

---

I also checked the decompression time for different levels and with or without LDM:

Level | LDM | Compressed size | Decompression time | Decompression throughput
--- | --- | --- | --- | ---
deflate-9 (master) | n/a | 28.08 MB | 177.6 ms | 0.72 GB/s
zstd-3 | off | 26.55 MB | 161.8 ms | 0.79 GB/s
zstd-3 | on | 19.96 MB | 205.7 ms | 0.63 GB/s
zstd-7 | off | 22.72 MB | 156.5 ms | 0.82 GB/s
zstd-7 | on | 16.97 MB | 206.6 ms | 0.62 GB/s
zstd-18 | off | 16.93 MB | 158.3 ms | 0.81 GB/s
zstd-18 | on | 12.99 MB | 207.3 ms | 0.62 GB/s
zstd-19 | off | 16.50 MB | 168.2 ms | 0.76 GB/s
zstd-19 | on | 12.72 MB | 210.5 ms | 0.61 GB/s
zstd-20 | off | 12.84 MB | 185.2 ms | 0.69 GB/s
zstd-20 | on | 12.68 MB | 200.4 ms | 0.64 GB/s

So it's worth noting that LDM adds ~30% to the decompression time, but it's still quite small (150 ms vs 200 ms at levels 3, 7 or 18). For the editor startup, this seems reasonable.

For comparison, the current decompression time in `master` with Deflate level 9 is measured at 177.6 ms on the same machine, so it's in the same ballpark. If we go with level 20 without LDM like in the current PR, we get 185.2ms, so we gain ~20ms compared to my proposed level 18 with LDM. Overall we're pretty much within margin of errors here, I think either option would be fine.

---

Finally I also did a sweep test on some of the zstd configuration options to see if we can have better gains, notably with the docs translation as base dataset as it's the biggest one with most redundant strings. I tested `window_log`, `ldm_min_match`, `ldm_hash_log`, `ldm_hash_rate_log`, and `ldm_bucket_size_log` and basically the defaults are already the best for our dataset.

> So I've done some fine-tuning of the compression to find good tradeoffs on compilation speed vs size reduction. I also tried enabling long-distance matching (LDM) which yields significant gains

Applied suggested patch.

So from all my findings so far, I would suggest this fine-tuning instead:
- Production: level 20, no LDM (back to original PR). The increase in build time is dwarfed by LTO linking, and so level 20 gives a slightly smaller binary and lower decompression time.
- Non-production, dev_build: level 7, no LDM. On a GB sized binary, the size doesn't matter, so let's avoid paying the ~50 ms extra decompression cost from LDM on dev builds we launch frequently.
- Non-production, optimized (kinda half-production): level 7, with LDM. Here the size gains are really worth it.

```diff
diff --git a/methods.py b/methods.py
index 0e1e66b459..5e48f4beab 100644
--- a/methods.py
+++ b/methods.py
@@ -1584,13 +1584,15 @@ def get_buffer(path: str) -> bytes:
 def compress_buffer_zstd(buffer: bytes, env):
     # Levels selected for a good tradeoff between compression speed and size reduction,
     # being more aggressive on production builds.
-    # Long-distance matching helps a lot with the editor translations.
-    level = 18 if env["production"] else 7
+    # Long-distance matching helps a lot with the editor translations on lower levels,
+    # but costs some extra decompression time (+30%). It's not helping at high levels.
+    level = 20 if env["production"] else 7
+    ldm = False if env["production"] or env.dev_build else True
     if sys.version_info >= (3, 14):
         import compression.zstd
 
         CP = compression.zstd.CompressionParameter
-        options = {CP.compression_level: level, CP.enable_long_distance_matching: 1}
+        options = {CP.compression_level: level, CP.enable_long_distance_matching: ldm}
         return compression.zstd.compress(buffer, options=options)
     else:
         try:
@@ -1598,7 +1600,7 @@ def compress_buffer_zstd(buffer: bytes, env):
         except ImportError:
             print_error("Python versions earlier than 3.14 require the `zstandard` module")
             sys.exit(255)
-        params = zstandard.ZstdCompressionParameters.from_level(level, enable_ldm=True)
+        params = zstandard.ZstdCompressionParameters.from_level(level, enable_ldm=ldm)
         return zstandard.ZstdCompressor(compression_params=params).compress(buffer)
 
 
```

And with that I think I've spent enough time micro-optimizing this :P
Thanks!

Install `zstandard` with `pip install zstandard` (might require `pip3` instead, depending on install), it is supported on Python 3.9+. 3.14+ have ZSTD included.
It probably makes sense to add `pip` command to the error message. But some systems now use externally managed Python environments (no sure how common it is), so it might cause more confusion.

> It probably makes sense to add `pip` command to the error message. But some systems now use externally managed Python environments (no sure how common it is), so it might cause more confusion.

`pip install --user zstandard` should be safe even on system-provided Python. This is a library rather than a binary, so it's fine if the installed package isn't available in `PATH` right away.

what about RAM consumption and startup speed?
why not measured vs .mo?

> what about RAM consumption and startup speed?

Decompression times were measured in https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/124108#issuecomment-6166461478

There's no difference between `mo` and `po`, neither is used directly and only serve as a source for `Translation` objects. In both new and old implementation, translations are decompressed into temporary buffer, parsed, and buffer is freed immediately after this.
